summary: David DiNardo recounts being laid off from the Ottawa Hospital at 24, shortly after finishing his MBA, and why he considers it the best thing that ever happened to him. The layoff pushed him into entrepreneurship and a promise never to let someone else control his trajectory. He shares four lessons from building and selling his business: being vulnerable in your personal brand, the tax advantage of dividends over salary in Canada, building your company as a sellable asset with the exit in mind, and enduring years of pain before the hockey-stick reward.
takeaways: Being laid off at 24 pushed David into entrepreneurship and a promise to never again let someone else have more control over his life than he did.
Vulnerability makes a personal brand relatable; a podcast is an easy way to have deeper conversations and clip out the vulnerable moments.
In Canada, a rising salary is eaten by higher tax brackets, while being incorporated lets you shelter money and decide how much to take out each year.
Every day of building a business is an investment in yourself as the asset; a sound operational engine is what attracted multiple buyers when David sold after 10 years.
Build with the exit in mind and know your industry's revenue multiple, since some businesses sell at one times revenue and others at two or even ten times.
It took David seven years to match his hospital salary, after which he tripled and then quadrupled it; entrepreneurship is a long slow grind before the hockey stick.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: I got laid off, and it was the best thing that ever happened to me. At 24 years old, starting my career out, working at the Ottawa Hospital, I thought that was gonna be my trajectory for the next 35 years. People around me were talking about their pensions, and that was the safe bet. I just graduated with my MBA, came and worked at the hospital, making really good money, getting paid every two weeks.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: That was the dream job, especially in Ottawa, until it wasn't, until someone had way more control and power over me, and I did not like it. I got let go at 24 years old, and it was the best thing that ever happened to me. Why? It pushed me into entrepreneurship. Would I have been an entrepreneur if that didn't happen to me?

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: Who knows. But I promised myself that day that I wouldn't work for someone, because I didn't want someone to have deeper control into my trajectory of my life than I did. So it was the best thing. And while building a personal brand, being vulnerable shows to the audience that you can be vulnerable and you can be relatable. And that's one thing while building this personal brand has really helped me.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: So if you're an entrepreneur out there and you're wanting to be vulnerable, do something like a podcast. Have deeper conversations where you don't have to speak in front of the camera. You could be speaking to someone and clip those vulnerability parts out so it's easier for you. The second thing that I really notice while building a business is salary versus dividends.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: When you work for someone, you're a salary employee. In Canada, that does not create wealth because the higher the salary goes, the higher your tax goes. When you're incorporated, you shelter the money, and you can dictate how much money you want per year. And what I realized while I was working at the hospital, I increased my salary, but I didn't net more money.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: Why? Because I got put in a different tax bracket, where when you're incorporated, you net more money. You can keep it in the corporation and only take it out when you wanna take it out. Huge advantage. Three, every day you're building yourself as the asset, not anyone else. You're putting content to yourself.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: You're building systems, processes, employees. You're building this engine for you to then it be worth something. And it took me over 10 years to build this engine to then sell and have multiple buyers wanting my business because the engine was so operationally sound, and that's so important because every day you're putting your energy and time into yourself, into your engine, into an asset that eventually will sell.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: I'm not saying all businesses do sell, but that's how you gotta think. And one thing that I always looked at from a mentor was always build your exit in mind, which means, hey, are you taking on a business that's one time multiple? You make $1 million, you could sell for a million dollars. Some industries are like that.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: Some industries are $1 million equals $2 million in future sell. So if you make $1 million in revenue, you could sell for $2 million. That's a two times multiple. Some are 10 times revenue. You make a million dollars, and you can sell for $10 million. So always think about the exit in mind while creating a business, and you'll be so far ahead.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: And finally, entrepreneurship, it's a lot of pain for a long period of time, and then you get the reward. It took me seven years to build a salary of what I was making at the hospital, knowing that I can take that money though and put it back into the business, and that's what I did. So even though it took seven years of a lot of problems, a lot of pain, a lot of suffering, at the seven-year mark, I made triple of what I made at the hospital, and then I quadrupled it.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: So it's a hockey stick. It goes smaller, and then it scales up. And even this podcast, it's been six months. It's a slow grind, but then it's gonna hit over time being consistent. And that, as an entrepreneur, that's what you gotta do. Those are a few examples of what I did in my career to be financially free at 34 years old.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: And if you're starting a business now today, do those four things. Really figure out your personal brand. There's gonna be a pivotal time in your life. There's gonna be times where you have to be consistent, and at the end of the day, you will have a story for yourself that you have to share and build that audience.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: Be authentic and go grow your small business.
